card.hook: Picture a cool day, warm water at about 38 to 40 °C, and steam curling up past grassy turf walls with the sea right behind. Sky Lagoon looks like a hobbit village that decided to take up spa days.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m north-east of Sky Lagoon, and face south-west. From here you can fit the low buildings, turf-covered edges and the sea into one shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole spa. Go to 0.5x for more sky and shoreline, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the turf walls and the cave entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the horizon on a third line, then tap the spa and slide it a touch darker if the sky or steam looks washed out.
card.best_time: Soft light near sunrise or sunset flatters the buildings and sky. In winter the low sun makes that glow last longer, and the spa lights can look lovely after dark if you use night mode and hold steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the infinity edge of the ocean-side pool, where the lagoon drops toward the North Atlantic. Use the front camera, rest your arms on the edge and let the open sea and horizon sit behind you. For a different frame, try beside the waterfall in the infinity pool.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone secure near the water. Frame shots so other guests are small or out of the picture, and check the official site before you go for any photography rules. Sky Lagoon is a spa and is likely to have ticketed, controlled entry.
card.challenge: Catch a wisp of steam drifting in front of the turf walls. Try a Live Photo and pick your best frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: Sky Lagoon sits at Kársnes Harbour in Kópavogur, the town next to Reykjavik. Building began in early 2020 and finished in 2021, and the design takes its cues from Icelandic landscape and heritage. You enter through a cave tunnel that leads to the hot soaking pool, and on a clear day you may spot Snæfellsjökull and the mountain Keilir.

card.hook: Look up from almost anywhere in central Reykjavík and there it is: a big, pale concrete tower poking above the rooftops like a rocket made of basalt columns. It's one bold shape, so your phone loves it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Frakkland, about 80 m north of the church, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The whole tower should rise up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower and the swept-back wings into one upright shot. Switch to 1x for a tidier, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the stepped concrete columns of the spire.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the pale concrete keeps its detail and the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is best, when the softer light shows off the texture in the concrete. A clear sky shows the shape of the tower best, so peek at the weather first.
card.selfie_here: Head to Hallgrímstorg square at the top of Skólavörðustígur and stand next to the Leifur Eiríksson statue on its tall stone pedestal. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the church directly behind you so the tower fills the background. For somewhere quieter, try the free sculpture garden at the Einar Jónsson Museum, standing among the sculptures with the tower rising behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the rainbow-painted stretch of Skólavörðustígur and shoot up the slope, while you stand on the painted street so the church sits at the top of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship with a lift to a viewing deck, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or entry rules.
card.challenge: Take one tall shot with a grid line running straight up the tower, then turn your phone sideways and see if you can fit both wings in. Bonus points if you can spot the 'basalt columns'.
card.good_to_know: Hallgrímskirkja is the largest church in Iceland and, at 74.5 metres, the second tallest building in the country. It's named after the poet and cleric Hallgrímur Pétursson. Building took 41 years, from 1945 to 1986, but the steeple and wings were finished in 1974, long before the nave was consecrated.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Frakkland, about 80 m north of the church, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The whole tower should rise up in front of you.

card.hook: Yes, it's exactly what you think it is, and the shopfront snap is the one your group chat will reply to first. Grab it from the pavement, then go in and see what the fuss is about.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the frontage as people see it. If the pavement is narrow and you can't fit it all in, tap 0.5x, and use 2x for a closer detail shot so you don't block the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's upright edges so the front looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest for a clear shot of the front. Early in the day is usually quieter on the pavement, so you get fewer strangers wandering through your picture.
card.selfie_here: Inside the museum, stand next to the big sperm whale specimen, its biggest exhibit and a popular selfie spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the exhibit behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside, usually without flash, but rules may apply, so ask staff or check the official site. The museum is ticketed, so check the site for entry details and the current address or entrance.
card.challenge: Get a straight-faced selfie in front of the museum, and see how long you can hold it before you giggle.
card.good_to_know: A retired teacher, Sigurður Hjartarson, founded the museum in 1997, and the collection began with a cattle whip made from a bull's penis. It spent several years in Húsavík and came back to Reykjavík in 2012 under his son, Hjörtur Gísli Sigurðsson. Today there are 280 specimens from 93 animal species, from a sperm whale's at 170 cm down to a hamster's at just 2 mm.

card.hook: Picture a glass bubble perched on a hill, balanced on top of giant hot water tanks. That's Perlan, and from a distance it's one of the easiest buildings in Reykjavik to spot in a phone frame.
card.stand_here: Head for Öskjuhlíð hill and look for the glass dome. The phone icon on the map marks the building itself, so step away from it, face the dome, and keep going until the whole curve of the glass and the tanks beneath it fit in your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the dome and tanks together from close range. Switch to zoom 1x for a more natural look once you've stepped back, then try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for details in the glass.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the tanks up with a horizontal line, so the building sits straight and doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day, when the light is soft and flatters the glass. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady to keep the shot sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooded walking paths on Öskjuhlíð hill around Perlan. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if you want more in, and stand with the glass dome and its tanks behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the forest trail below the building, where the whole glass dome and the tanks fit in the frame, while you pose with Perlan behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The observation deck can be very windy, so bring a warm jacket and gloves. Check the official site for access and opening details before you go.
card.challenge: Fill the frame with the glass pattern against the sky, then take a second shot of the line where the dome meets the tanks.
card.good_to_know: Perlan is also called The Pearl. The tanks were first built in 1939 to store hot water for the city. The building opened to the public on 21 June 1991, and now holds a museum, a planetarium, an ice cave and an observation deck.

card.hook: Walk up close to Harpa and the whole wall turns into a giant puzzle of coloured glass, with the sky and the people walking past tucked inside the panels. It's inspired by Iceland's basalt, so it looks a bit like a block of cut crystal.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near Hörputorg and stand about 20 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west, then take a step or two to each side until you find a line of panels you love.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, since you're so close. Switch to zoom 1x for cleaner, less stretched glass, then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a few panels as an abstract pattern.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a bright panel, then slide the picture a touch darker so the sky reflections don't wash out.
card.best_time: After dark, the 714 LED lights on the front add colour to your shots, so try night mode and keep your elbows tucked against your body to hold the phone still. Overcast days still work well for close-ups of the panels.
card.selfie_here: Stand right up against Harpa's harbour-side glass, use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, look up and let the honeycomb panels fill the background behind you. card.ask_someone: Stand about halfway up the harbour-facing staircase on the north side inside Harpa and ask a passer-by to shoot from below, so the stairs, you and the glass front all fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos in the public foyer are fine, but not during private or ticketed events, and staff will tell you if it's not allowed. Indoors, keep clear of stairs and event entrances.
card.challenge: Find one panel that has caught a stranger's reflection and make a picture with no sky at all.
card.good_to_know: Harpa is Reykjavik's concert hall and conference centre, and the opening concert was on 4 May 2011. The Danish firm Henning Larsen Architects designed it together with the artist Olafur Eliasson. In 2013 it won the European Union's Mies van der Rohe award for contemporary architecture.

card.hook: Picture a ship that's lost its walls and decided to sail anyway. That's the Sun Voyager: shiny steel ribs on a little headland, with the sea showing right through them.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon near Mánaleið, about 55 m west of the sculpture, and face east. From there you get the whole ship with sea and sky around it. Then stroll over to the granite circle for closer angles.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole ship with sea and sky. Drop to 0.5x for a low, dramatic view from down by the base. Use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the curving steel ribs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the ship on one line and leave lots of sky, then tap the steel and slide to darker if the sky is bright so the steel keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Evening or early morning, when the sun is low, gives softer light on the steel. At sunset you get warm light on it too.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the east side of the sculpture, on the waterfront paving, and turn so the ship is roughly three-quarters on behind you with its prow pointing out toward Mount Esja across the bay. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold the phone low and kneel a bit so the steel sweeps up over your shoulder. Check the ship is actually behind you on screen before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back along the raised part of the Sæbraut waterfront path, not right by the steel, while you stand at the base, so the whole sculpture fits with the bay and mountains behind. It's a bit vague, so check the spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no barriers, but please don't climb the sculpture: oils from hands dull the steel and it wasn't built to hold weight. Stay on the paving, because the steel can get slippery in rain, ice or sea spray.
card.challenge: Find an angle where you can see the sea through the ribs and make it look like the ship is floating.
card.good_to_know: Sun Voyager (Sólfar in Icelandic) is by artist Jón Gunnar Árnason, who called it a dreamboat and an ode to the Sun. It was made for Reykjavík's 200th anniversary, won a competition in 1986 and was unveiled on 18 August 1990. He knew it would face north rather than toward the setting sun, and he was fine with that.

card.hook: A painted street does half your work for you, because your eye just slides along the stripes. Even a quick snap ends up with a clear subject and a sense of depth.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Skólavörðustígur, and face south-east. Keep to the pavement while you line up your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the street. Want more buildings in the frame? Try zoom 0.5x, or zoom 2x if your phone has it to squeeze the street so the colours look closer together.

card.rules_and_safety: The street slopes uphill and can be icy in winter, so wear shoes with good grip. Stay on the pavement while you line up shots.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the stripes run straight into the picture with no bins, signs or parked vehicles poking in at the edges.
card.good_to_know: Rainbow Street is the name on our map for Skólavörðustígur, a street in Reykjavik. Some guides describe the rainbow paint as permanent and others say it's repainted for Pride, so it may look a bit different when you visit. Check locally before you go, as road works or events may change access.

card.hook: Picture a rainbow-painted street climbing straight up to a big stone church, with nothing in the way but a few people on their coffee break. That's the view everyone's after on Laugavegur.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Laugavegur and Skólavörðustígur, at the lower end of the rainbow-painted stretch, and face uphill. Hallgrímskirkja sits at the far end, and the marked point on Laugavegur is to the south-east of where you stand.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the junction and the painted road. Try 0.5x to fit in the full width of the street, but keep the church centred so the edges don't stretch. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) pulls the church closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the painted road, then slide the picture darker if the sky and church look washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning is the quietest, so you get the fewest people in your shot. For the view down Laugavegur itself, with its colourful shopfronts, late afternoon is a good bet.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the rainbow-painted stretch where Laugavegur meets Skólavörðustígur, switch to the front camera and try 0.5x, then turn so Hallgrímskirkja is over your shoulder. For another bright backdrop, the mural-covered bakery front on Frakkastígur is a short turn off Laugavegur.
card.rules_and_safety: These are open public streets, so wait a moment for passers-by to clear the frame and keep out of the way of people walking.
card.challenge: Get the painted road running dead centre, with the church perched at the top like a cherry on a cake, and not a single stranger in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Laugavegur means 'wash road'. It once led to the hot springs in Laugardalur, where local women took their laundry. The street was built in 1885, and on Friday and Saturday nights it's often busy until late.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Laugavegur and Skólavörðustígur, at the lower end of the rainbow-painted stretch, and face uphill. Hallgrímskirkja sits at the far end, and the marked point on Laugavegur is to the south-east of where you stand.

card.hook: Dark stone, a calm symmetrical front, and a lawn and trees to set it off: Alþingishúsið is the kind of building that looks good almost without trying. Your only job is to not let a stranger's head wander into the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lawn of Austurvöllur, the square directly in front of the building, and face the front of the Parliament House. Back up until the whole façade fits comfortably on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full front of the building. Use 0.5x only if people or trees force you to stand close. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the window reliefs and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the façade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the dark stone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Morning light gives clean, even photos of the façade, and late afternoon adds warmer tones to the stone. For the wider street-and-square view from Kirkjutorg, evening light is lovely.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Jón Sigurðsson statue in the square, use the front camera (try 0.5x if the building won't fit) and hold it out so the Parliament House sits behind you. Want it quieter? Try the garden at the back of the building, with the rear of the house behind you. Both spots are suggestions from photo guides, so check them on site.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the lawn of Austurvöllur facing the façade, while you stand between them and the house, so they get the full building behind you (it works best when it's not too crowded).
card.rules_and_safety: In winter the paving around Austurvöllur can be uneven and slippery, so take care when posing. Keep clear of the entrances and any security areas.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the first-floor windows and hunt down all four guardian spirits of Iceland: a dragon, a vulture, a giant and a bull.
card.good_to_know: Alþingishúsið still houses Alþingi, the Icelandic parliament. It was designed by Ferdinand Meldahl and built from hewn Icelandic dolerite between 1880 and 1881. Over the years it has also housed the National Library, the National Gallery, parts of the University of Iceland and, until 1973, the President's offices.

card.hook: A bronze Viking stands on the prow of a granite ship, and a huge pale church is parked right behind him like he planned it. Dark figure, light tower, clear sky: your phone will love this one.
card.stand_here: Head for Hallgrímstorg, the square in front of Hallgrímskirkja, about 1 minute on foot to the south. Stand close to the base of the pedestal and face the church, so Leif is in front and the whole tower fits behind him.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue and church together. If you can step back, try zoom 2x so the church looks bigger behind him, and use zoom 0.5x only when you're right at the pedestal and want the full height of the church.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze figure, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so Leif doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in your shot. Sunset is said to give softer light on the bronze.
card.selfie_here: On the paved square at the foot of the bow-shaped pedestal, use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and tilt up a little so the statue and tower fit over your shoulder. You can also stand on the sloping part of the plaza facing downhill toward the city, with the monument behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask them to stand back on the open square, a little to the left or right of the statue, so you, the bronze figure and the church all fit in one frame.
card.challenge: Take one shot with people in it and one without, then pick which one makes Leif look more like the explorer of the square.
card.good_to_know: The statue is by the American sculptor Alexander Stirling Calder. The United States gave it to Iceland for the 1,000th anniversary of the Alþingi, the Icelandic parliament, in 1930. It was unveiled on 17 July 1932, and the Texas red granite pedestal is about 4.6 metres high.

card.hook: Picture a calm green lawn in the middle of town, with a church and a Parliament building sitting side by side like neighbours. That's the whole charm of this spot, and it fits in one easy phone shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open lawn of Austurvöllur, the green square in the old city centre, and face the cathedral across the grass. The Parliament House (Alþingishúsið) sits right beside it, so keep both in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the cathedral and the Parliament House together. If you're standing close or want more sky and grass, try 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for a closer shot of the church front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the cathedral on one of the vertical lines and let the Parliament House fill the other side.
card.best_time: Early morning is the suggested time for quieter views and cleaner shots of the buildings around the square.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it up a little so the cathedral rises over your shoulder. Hold the phone slightly higher than your face and take a few, because the first one is never the best.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral may be closed outside posted hours, so check the official site before you go. Austurvöllur itself is an open public square.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide with the church and Parliament House as neighbours, then one close-up of the church alone. Which one would you put on the fridge?
card.good_to_know: The first cathedral here was built in 1787 to a design by the royal building inspector Andreas Hallander. It was pulled down in 1847 to make way for a somewhat larger church. Since Iceland's parliament, the Alþingi, was revived in 1845, each session has opened with a Mass here, after which the dean leads the members of parliament across to the Parliament House.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open lawn of Austurvöllur, the green square in the old city centre, and face the cathedral across the grass. The Parliament House (Alþingishúsið) sits right beside it, so keep both in the frame.

card.hook: Picture a little white timber house sitting calmly by the Reykjavik shore, looking far too modest for the day in 1986 when Reagan and Gorbachev met inside it. The sea does half the work for your photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Sæbraut waterfront walk, approaching Höfði from the west. From here the house is just to the south, so face south with the sea and shoreline leading your eye toward it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the sea, the shoreline and the house all fit in one frame. Want the house bigger without walking closer? Try 2x. In the grounds, 0.5x gives you lots of sky above the white front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the shoreline along a lower line and the house on one of the vertical lines, then tap the white walls and slide it a touch darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or evening light is kinder to the white walls than harsh midday sun. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the grass around the house on the seaward side: use the front camera, stand with the house behind you and the bay opening out in front. Step a few paces around the grounds to find a clean background, or pose by the Einar Benediktsson monument next to the house. Both spots are worth a quick check on the day.

card.rules_and_safety: The inside is generally closed, so photograph the exterior from the grounds and public paths, and respect any temporary barriers or official events. Mind the wind gusts near the water.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the shoreline points straight at the house and keep the horizon dead level. Bonus points if Mount Esja sneaks into the background.
card.good_to_know: Höfði was built in 1909 for the French consul, Jean-Paul Brillouin. It was prefabricated in Norway, shipped to Iceland and put up on the site. The city bought it in 1958, and it's best known for the 1986 Reykjavík Summit.

card.hook: Picture a stall of dried cod, pickled herring and fermented shark, and you pointing your phone at it with a very brave face. Welcome to Kolaportið, Iceland's only flea market, where the details are the show.
card.stand_here: Head for Kolaportið, the old Customs building by the harbour in central Reykjavík. The phone icon on the map sits right at the building, so you can start shooting the moment you step inside. Keep to the side of the aisle so you don't block anyone.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for stalls and aisles. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for records, jars and food, so you don't crowd the stallholder. In a tight aisle try 0.5x, but keep people away from the edges of the frame, where faces can look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Tap on your subject, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright lamps don't wash out the stalls.
card.best_time: The market is normally open only at weekends, Saturday and Sunday from 11:00 to 17:00, and closed Monday to Friday. Check the official site first that it's still running, because the building's future has been uncertain.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and step back from a colourful stall so it sits over your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the scene fits in with you. Stand near a door or a bright lamp, because the light inside can be dim.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed for personal use, but ask before taking close-ups of a stallholder or their goods. Keep your bag close and don't block the aisles while you compose your shot.
card.challenge: Find one row of records, books or clothes that makes the aisle lead the eye, then zoom in on the single item you'd take home.
card.good_to_know: Kolaportið opened in 1989 in the city parking garage under a bank building. In 1994 it moved into the Customs House. In 2024 the City of Reykjavik decided to move the University of the Arts into the building and began a search for new premises for the market. No suitable site was found, so the market was extended to at least March 2025.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Kolaportið, the old Customs building by the harbour in central Reykjavík. The phone icon on the map sits right at the building, so you can start shooting the moment you step inside. Keep to the side of the aisle so you don't block anyone.

card.hook: Fun fact to start: this calm, solid building was a freezing plant before it was an art museum. Cold storage has had a glow-up.
card.stand_here: Stand near Skálholtsstígur, about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west and the gallery is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole building in. Use 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out a doorway or a window, and drop to 0.5x if you step closer and the front won't fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the walls with them so the building doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day the light is softer and kinder to the walls than harsh midday sun. Winter days are short, so check daylight hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the eastern bank of the Tjörnin pond, on the lakeside path by the gallery, with the building behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and tilt up a touch so the gallery fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the north shore of Tjörnin on the lakeside path and centre the gallery's white stone facade in the frame, so its reflection fills the lower half of the picture, while you pose in the shot.

card.hook: The smallest thing on this street gets the longest line. A little hot dog stand with a queue of hungry people in front of it is a much better Reykjavik photo than you'd expect.
card.stand_here: Cross to the far side of Tryggvagata, the side facing the Harpa Concert Hall. From there the stand is a short way to the south-west, so face it and you're looking back across the road at its front and the queue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the stand, the queue and a bit of street. If the pavement is crowded and you can't step back, drop to zoom 0.5x. Try zoom 2x to pick out the sign and the serving hatch from across the road.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stand, then slide the brightness a little darker so the white sign doesn't glare.
card.best_time: Go when the queue is short and the stand is easier to see. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement on the Harpa side of Tryggvagata, with the stand's red front behind you. Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x so more of the stand fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the pavement across Tryggvagata from the stand, then pose by the stand so its whole front and you fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is an open street on a public road, but the stand is a food business, so check the official site before you go for when it's serving.
card.challenge: Get a close-up of someone holding a hot dog "with everything" (with their permission), with the stand's sign blurry in the background.
card.good_to_know: Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur means "The Town's Best Hot Dogs", and the chain has run since 1937, when the first stand opened on Austurstræti. In the 1960s it moved to Tryggvagata, across from Harpa, and the main stand is still there. Bill Clinton visited in 2004, and in 2006 The Guardian named it the best hot dog stand in Europe.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Cross to the far side of Tryggvagata, the side facing the Harpa Concert Hall. From there the stand is a short way to the south-west, so face it and you're looking back across the road at its front and the queue.

card.hook: A concrete hall that looks like it's floating on a pond, with a swan or duck drifting past in front. Honestly, it's hard to take a bad photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stretch of pond shore near Tjarnargata, where the City Hall sits. Face across Tjörnin so the hall and the downtown rooftops behind it fill your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole pond, the hall and the town together. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched hall, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for reflections or birds on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the water's edge on a lower line so the reflection fills the bottom third, and let the hall sit off to one side.
card.best_time: Go on a calm, dry day, because still water gives you the clearest reflection. Walk a little way along the shore too, as the hall's angles and its reflection change with every few steps.
card.selfie_here: Try the pond-side footpath that runs along Tjörnin behind the hall, or the small bridge over the pond that leads to the hall's entrance. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the hall in over your shoulder so its low shape and reflection fill the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stay by the pond near Tjarnargata, where they can look across Tjörnin at the hall, and pose with the water and the hall behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The paths beside the pond can be icy in winter, so watch your footing while you look at the screen. If the pond is partly frozen, keep well away from thin ice.
card.challenge: Wait for a bird to drift into the foreground and get it sharp with the hall soft behind it. Bonus points if the swan looks like it's posing.
card.good_to_know: The hall was completed in 1992 after an international competition won by the architects Studio Granda. Inside are the mayor's offices and a large 3D map of Iceland. It's sometimes used for art exhibitions, functions and live music.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the stretch of pond shore near Tjarnargata, where the City Hall sits. Face across Tjörnin so the hall and the downtown rooftops behind it fill your view.

card.hook: Picture a pond in the middle of a capital city, with greylag geese bobbing about and a white church standing at the water's edge. That's Tjörnin, and it's very easy to love.
card.stand_here: Head for Fríkirkjuvegur on the east bank of the pond, next to the white Free Church (Fríkirkjan). Face the water so the downtown buildings rise up behind it, and walk a few steps either way along the street until the water fills the bottom of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the water, church and skyline all in one go. Switch to 0.5x if you want more sky and shoreline, or 2x (or more, depending on your phone) to pick out City Hall or the birds without walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the far shore on the upper third line, so the water gets most of the picture and the church sits at one edge like a frame.
card.best_time: Check whether the pond has frozen before you go. In winter the scene looks quite different, and the water's edge can be harder to reach.
card.selfie_here: Go to the southern end of the pond where it meets Hljómskálagarður park, turn your back to the water and use the front camera. Try 0.5x so you get you, the lake and the greener park backdrop in one shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the little footbridge by City Hall to take your photo, with you framed against the water and City Hall.
card.rules_and_safety: If the pond is frozen, you may not be able to get close to the water's edge. One visitor advises being careful on the ice in winter and keeping away from unfrozen patches.
card.challenge: Take a few frames with a bird in the foreground and the church behind it. Bonus points if the bird actually looks at the camera.
card.good_to_know: Tjörnin simply means "the pond", and it's shallow, with an average depth of about half a metre. Between 40 and 50 species of water bird have been recorded here, including Arctic terns, eiders, greylag geese and whooper swans. City Hall sits in the north-west corner and looks as though it's rising out of the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Fríkirkjuvegur on the east bank of the pond, next to the white Free Church (Fríkirkjan). Face the water so the downtown buildings rise up behind it, and walk a few steps either way along the street until the water fills the bottom of your screen.

card.hook: This church doesn't need to shout. Its simple, clear shape stands out against the open space by Tjörnin, and on a still day the lake gives it a calm picture frame.
card.stand_here: Stand near Bæjarleið, at the phone icon on the map, about 35 m south-west of the church. Face north-east and the whole building should sit comfortably in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole church with a little of its surroundings. Then try 2x for the entrance and the front of the building. Only use 0.5x if you step closer and want to fit everything in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the church up with the vertical lines so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Pick a calm moment when the lake surface is still, because the water makes a lovely foreground. If people wander through, wait a moment and take a few frames in a row.
card.selfie_here: Try the Tjörnin shore on the Fríkirkjuvegur side, right beside the church. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and tilt so the church sits over your shoulder, then check the framing on the spot to make sure it made it in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the City Hall shore of the pond, looking across the water at the church, to take your photo while you stand by the lake near the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is usually closed to visitors, so plan to photograph it from outside. If you want to go in, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the church and its watery twin share the frame, with not a single stranger in it. Patience is the secret.
card.good_to_know: Fríkirkjan is a Lutheran church that stands independently of the Church of Iceland. The congregation was founded in autumn 1899, and the church was consecrated on 22 February 1903. It was lengthened only two years later, then enlarged again in 1924 with a concrete chancel at the eastern end.

card.hook: Picture a patch of grass with cafés around it, a big bronze statue in the middle and Iceland's Parliament standing right behind. That's Austurvöllur, and it hands you a person, a building and a bit of history in one tidy frame.
card.stand_here: Walk to the middle of Austurvöllur, where the phone icon on the map is. Face the statue of Jón Sigurðsson so the Parliament House (Alþingishúsið) sits behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the statue with Parliament behind it. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. Then turn around and use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Hallgrímskirkja in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the Parliament House with a horizontal line so it looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go before about 10 a.m., when the lawn is quieter and the light is nicer on the statue and Parliament. Take a few shots in case people wander through your frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand by the Jón Sigurðsson statue on the lawn in the middle of the square, with the Parliament House behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the building in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn across from Alþingishúsið while you stand with the building behind you, and ask them to widen the shot if you'd like the cathedral in too.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is sometimes used for gatherings and protests, so check before you go if you need a clear view on a particular day. In winter, wind can funnel through the streets around the square and surfaces can be slippery.
card.challenge: Get the statue, Parliament and a café in one shot, then spin around and find Hallgrímskirkja in the distance with your zoom.
card.good_to_know: Jón Sigurðsson was a leader of Iceland's independence movement. Next to the square is Dómkirkjan, the city's oldest church. In the early 18th century the square was much larger, and a statue of Bertel Thorvaldsen once stood where Jón Sigurðsson stands now.
